summary: The Eastern Gangas had ruled a small kingdom in southern Kalinga from Kalinganagara since about 500, and in the 11th century Vajrahasta V and Rajaraja I turned it into a regional power. Anantavarman Chodaganga (1078–1150) conquered Utkala, ruled from the Ganges to the Godavari and began the Jagannath temple at Puri. His successors held off the Muslim rulers of Bengal, and Narasimhadeva I (1238–1264) struck at Lakhnauti and built the Sun Temple at Konark, but the dynasty declined after him and was ended by the usurper Kapilendra in 1434.
details: The Eastern Gangas, probably an offshoot of the Western Gangas of Karnataka, had ruled part of Kalinga, on India's east coast, since about 500, with their capital at Kalinganagara (Mukhalingam). For centuries they were a minor dynasty, often under stronger neighbours. Vajrahasta V, king from 1038 to about 1070, revived their fortunes. He took the grand titles Trikalingadhipati and Sakalakalingadhipati, 'lord of the three Kalingas' and 'lord of all Kalinga', challenged the Somavamshi kings to the north and allied with the Kalachuris.

Vajrahasta's son Rajaraja Deva I (c. 1070–1077) pushed Ganga power further. He defeated the Somavamshi king of Utkala to the north and extended his authority towards the Vengi region to the south. His relations with the mighty Chola empire mixed war and diplomacy: he married a Chola princess, Rajasundari, a daughter of the emperor Virarajendra. Their son, half Ganga and half Chola, would become the greatest king of the dynasty, Anantavarman Chodaganga, whose name joins both lines.

Anantavarman Chodaganga succeeded his father on 17 February 1078 (some lists say 1077), and by his own inscription he reigned for 72 years. In his early years the Cholas attacked and for a time took the Visakhapatnam district, but he recovered his lands. He then turned to expansion. Over the following decades he made the Gangas the dominant power of the eastern coast, ruling from the Godavari in the south to Midnapore in Bengal in the north, between the Bay of Bengal and the Eastern Ghats.

North of Kalinga lay Utkala, the heart of modern Odisha, ruled by the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings. According to the Madalapanji, the chronicle of the Puri temple, Chodaganga defeated the last Kesari king and moved his capital to Chaudwar-Cuttack on the Mahanadi. The conquest is dated to about 1112, and a grant of 1118 claims sovereignty over all of Utkala. It united Kalinga and Utkala into a single kingdom, roughly the Odisha of later history, and shifted the dynasty's centre north from Kalinganagara.

Chodaganga, a Shaiva by birth, turned to Vaishnavism, reportedly under the influence of the teacher Ramanuja. He began the present temple of Jagannath, a form of Vishnu, at Puri on the coast of Utkala. Its start is not dated exactly: an inscription of 1134–1135 records his donation, so building probably began between 1112 and the 1130s, and it was completed around 1150–1161. The temple became the religious heart of the kingdom and one of the holiest pilgrimage sites in India, famous for its Ratha Yatra chariot festival.

Late in his reign Chodaganga attacked Bengal after the death of the Pala king Ramapala, defeated the king of Mandara and destroyed the fortified town of Aramya, possibly Arambagh in Hooghly. He also took the part of Vengi north of the Godavari. He died around 1150 (some sources say 1147), and his kingdom was described as reaching from the Ganges to the Godavari. His successors, Kamarnava, Raghava, Rajaraja II and Anangabhima II, ruled quietly for half a century, though Kamarnava failed to win Sambalpur from the Kalachuris of Ratanpur.

At the start of the 13th century Turkish commanders from north India conquered western Bengal and made Lakhnauti their capital, bringing Muslim rule to the Ganga kingdom's northern border. In 1205, in the reign of Rajaraja Deva III, Muhammad Sheran Khalji advanced towards Lakhnauti in what was the first Muslim incursion threatening the kingdom, but he withdrew without invading Odisha. For the rest of the dynasty's history, the Bengal frontier was its most dangerous border, and the Ganga kings had to defend their kingdom against repeated attacks from the north.

Anangabhima Deva III (1211–1238) ruled from the Ganga river to the Godavari. With his general and minister Vishnu he beat back invasions by Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Shah, the ruler of Bengal. He defeated the Kalachuris of Ratanpur and took the Sambalpur–Bolangir region. He founded a new capital at Cuttack, at the meeting of the Mahanadi and Kathajodi rivers, with the Barabati fort. He also dedicated his kingdom to Jagannath and called himself the god's deputy, making the deity of Puri the divine sovereign of Odisha.

In the south the Kakatiya kings of Telangana were expanding. In the 1230s the Kakatiya ruler Ganapati Deva brought the Godavari and Krishna deltas under his control, and his power reached into the Ganjam district of southern Odisha. Anangabhima III fought the Kakatiyas, but they took territory up to the East Godavari region. The southern frontier, which under Chodaganga had lain on the Godavari, was pushed back, and the Telugu coastal lands were lost to the Gangas.

Anangabhima's son Narasimhadeva I (1238–1264) chose to attack rather than wait. In 1242–1243 his army marched against Tughral Tughan Khan, the Delhi Sultanate's governor of Bengal, and took control of Rarh, west of the Hooghly. When Tughan counter-attacked, the Odia forces met him near Katasin (Contai) with trenches, hidden troops and a feigned retreat, and a surprise attack inflicted heavy losses; Tughan narrowly escaped. It was one of the few defeats inflicted on the Bengal sultanate's armies in that era.

Following up his victory, Narasimhadeva sent his army deep into Bengal in 1244. It took two provinces and surrounded the fort of Lakhnauti, the capital, and the Muslim commander Fakhr-ul-Mulk Karimuddin Laghri was killed. Tughan Khan appealed to Delhi, and the governor of Awadh, Tamur Khan, arrived with reinforcements, so the siege was short. Tughan was removed and Tamur took over Bengal. Narasimhadeva's campaign kept the Muslim rulers of Bengal on the defensive and secured Odisha's northern frontier for decades.

In a 1246 inscription Narasimhadeva became the first Odisha king to use the title Gajapati, 'lord of elephants', which later rulers of Odisha kept for centuries. Around 1250 he built the great temple of Surya, the sun god, at Konark on the coast, reportedly to celebrate his victories over Bengal. It was designed as a colossal stone chariot pulled by seven horses on 24 carved wheels. Its main tower, once over 60 metres high, has collapsed, but the temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a masterpiece of Odisha's architecture.

Narasimhadeva I died in 1264, and with him ended the dynasty's age of conquest. His successors, Bhanu Deva I, Narasimha Deva II, Bhanu Deva II and Narasimha Deva III, held Odisha for almost another century, but they were mostly on the defensive against the Delhi Sultanate, its governors in Bengal and the powers of the south. In the 1350s Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq invaded and levied tribute. The last king, Bhanu Deva IV, was overthrown in 1434–35 by his minister Kapilendra, founder of the Gajapati dynasty.
